solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Where to see Etonians gain military award, right?

parts.note: to win = to gain
DSO = Distinguished Service Order, a British military decoration
R = right

explanation.surface: A question about spotting old Etonians who have picked up medals for bravery.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton College stands just across the Thames from Windsor, so that is where you see Etonians.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton sits beside Windsor, so Windsor is the place to see its pupils.

clue.text: Condiment is no longer somewhat timeless

parts.note: what is no longer, was
somewhat = A BIT; without its T (time) it is A BI

explanation.surface: A wistful remark that a condiment has lost its timeless quality.
explanation.walkthrough: Timeless is split in two: T is time, and 'less' removes it from A BIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Wasabi is the hot green Japanese paste served with sushi.

clue.text: Return of police force? A day is not settled

indicators.note: a return sends the pieces back the other way

parts.note: CID = Criminal Investigation Department
A as printed
MON = Monday

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether the police force will come back, as nothing has been settled.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole string CID + A + MON is read backwards, not just the police force.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomadic people move about rather than settling in one place.

clue.text: American's knockout has failed, punching morose drunk

indicators.note: punching means driving into, so the shuffled has goes inside the other shuffled word
drunk means reeling, so the letters of morose are rearranged
failed means broken down, so the letters of has are rearranged

explanation.surface: A US boxer's punch has missed, hitting a gloomy drunkard.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are scrambled here: 'failed' works on has, 'drunk' on morose, and the first result sits inside the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Smasheroo is American slang for a smash hit or a huge success, a knockout.

clue.text: Are you texting personnel in mining area?

indicators.note: text-speak writes 'are you' as R U

parts.note: R U = are you in a text message
HR = human resources, the personnel department

explanation.surface: Someone texts to ask whether you are working in HR at a mine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ruhr is Germany's great coal-mining and industrial valley.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ruhr valley was famous for its coal mines.

clue.text: Giving a wave to page, monarch and imperial family

parts.note: p = page
ER = Elizabeth Regina
the Ming dynasty ruled China

explanation.surface: Royals waving to a page, as at a court ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: The royal wave is a false trail: the wave is put into hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairdresser's perm sets curls or waves into straight hair, so the wave is a hairstyle, not a gesture.

clue.text: Following delivery job with role outside in uniform

parts.note: a post = a job
a part = a role

indicators.note: take the outside letters of the word that follows

parts.note: outer letters of UniforM

explanation.surface: A delivery driver takes a job that means wearing a uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: Delivery here is childbirth, not parcels.
explanation.definitionFit: Postpartum means after giving birth.

clue.text: Rolls filled by kiddies regularly for traveller

indicators.note: filled by means having something put inside, so the car letters take in the picked letters

parts.note: RR is Rolls-Royce, the car maker

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so alternate letters of kiddies are taken

explanation.surface: Bread rolls are stuffed by children at intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolls' looks like bread; it is RR, Rolls-Royce. Alternate letters of KIDDIES give IDE.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider is someone travelling on a horse, bicycle or vehicle, so a traveller.

clue.text: Individually specify setter on cryptic Times puzzle finally

parts.note: the setter speaks of themself as I

indicators.note: TIMES is made obscure, so rearranged

parts.note: TIMES rearranged

indicators.note: at the end, so the last letter of the word it follows

parts.note: last letter of puzzlE

explanation.surface: A setter listing exactly what went into a cryptic Times puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about this very crossword, which hides that 'setter' just means I.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to specify things individually is to list them item by item.

clue.text: General meaning to keep artillerymen back, and a good mechanic

indicators.note: to keep means the general and meaning hold the other letters between them

parts.note: G is an abbreviation for general
the gist of something is its meaning

indicators.note: back means the artillerymen's letters are written in reverse

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, the British Army's gunners

explanation.surface: An army officer wants to retain his gunners in the rear, and a skilled repairman.
explanation.walkthrough: G is the abbreviation for General, and the Royal Artillery are Britain's army gunners. Garagist is a mostly British word for someone who runs or works in a garage.
explanation.definitionFit: A garagist is a person who runs or works in a garage repairing cars.

clue.text: Experienced fellow feeling stymied has cracked, admitting pressure

indicators.note: the letters break and re-form

parts.note: anagram fodder
p = pressure, added to the fodder

explanation.surface: A frustrated man cracks under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: Fellow feeling is a phrase for sympathy, not a man's emotions.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'fellow feeling' is an old phrase for sympathy, so experiencing it is a verb for sympathy.

clue.text: Some corn whiskey dropped by Don

indicators.note: something dropped is let fall

parts.note: to don = to wear, as clothes
W is whiskey in the phonetic alphabet; this letter is dropped

explanation.surface: Some corn whiskey gets spilled by a man called Don.
explanation.walkthrough: Don is the verb 'put on', not a name; WEAR loses its W to leave EAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A cereal-farming term: an ear is the grain-bearing head of the corn plant.

clue.text: Eastern ascetic from China curtailed expression of triumph

indicators.note: 'curtailed' cuts a letter off

parts.note: BUDDY is what 'China' stands for
Ha! as a cry of triumph

explanation.surface: A holy man from China crying out in victory.
explanation.walkthrough: China means mate, from rhyming slang 'china plate'; the country is a false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: The Buddha renounced worldly comfort and lived as an ascetic in India.

clue.text: What choirs do, covering eg Scarborough Fair

parts.note: start of SING
Scarborough is a Yorkshire seaside port

explanation.surface: Choirs singing the folk song Scarborough Fair.
explanation.walkthrough: The song title splits in two: Scarborough is an example of a port, and Fair is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in its games sense: playing fair is being sporting towards an opponent.

clue.text: Capers perhaps in creamy dish, in book put on line

indicators.note: put on means placed on top in this down clue, so the book part sits above the line
in means placed inside, so the dessert goes within the word for book

parts.note: a tome is a large book
a fool is a dessert of fruit folded into cream
RY is the abbreviation for railway, a line

explanation.surface: Capers might be added to a creamy dish, according to a recipe book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capers' looks like the pickled buds in a dish; it means antics, and 'perhaps' marks them as one example of tomfoolery.
explanation.definitionFit: Capers are playful antics or pranks, and tomfoolery is silly, foolish behaviour.

clue.text: Drinkers seizing last of beer obtained capacious bags

indicators.note: seizing means grabbing hold of, so the drinkers word holds the other letters

parts.note: carousers are people drinking and making merry
got means obtained

indicators.note: last of means the final letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Revellers grab the remaining beer and fill their roomy bags.
explanation.walkthrough: CAROUSERS holds GOT and R: CAR + GOTR + OUSERS. Bags is British slang for trousers, as in Oxford bags.
explanation.definitionFit: Cargo trousers are loose trousers with large pockets, and bags is an old word for baggy trousers.

clue.text: Say Mark is with East German Max

parts.note: to utter = to say
m = mark, the old German currency
Ost is German for east

explanation.surface: Introducing a man named Mark who is with an East German called Max.
explanation.walkthrough: Max is not a name but short for maximum, an adjective here.
explanation.definitionFit: Max as in 'to the max' means the uttermost, the furthest extent.

clue.text: Showing versatility, fitting into a seedy establishment

parts.note: start of A DIVE, a seedy bar
apt = fitting

explanation.surface: Someone adapts well by fitting in at a dodgy bar.
explanation.walkthrough: A dive is a disreputable bar or club.
explanation.definitionFit: Being adaptive means adjusting readily, which shows versatility.

clue.text: Damned academic's way to make two lots of us fat?

definitions.meaning: Marlowe's scholar who sold his soul to the devil

definitions.text: way to make two lots of us fat?
definitions.meaning: read the answer as an instruction: 'doctor' means rearrange, and the letters of the surname rearrange into US + US + FAT

explanation.surface: A worry that some damned professor's methods will fatten the two of us.
explanation.walkthrough: This works backwards: the answer read as an anagram instruction, doctor FAUSTUS, produces US US FAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctor Faustus, in Marlowe's play, is a scholar damned for his pact with the devil.

clue.text: Division of a real firm accepting case of evasion over raised tax

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the firm letters hold the rest

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

indicators.note: over means placed above in this down clue, so the case letters come first
case of means the outer letters, the shell, of the word that follows
raised means lifted up, so in a down clue the tax is read from the bottom up

parts.note: VAT is value added tax

explanation.surface: A firm takes in evaded money and lifts taxes, on a slice of a Spanish royal sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A real' looks like the adjective; the real is Brazil's currency, divided into a hundred of these.
explanation.definitionFit: A centavo is a hundredth of the Brazilian real, a small coin subdividing the currency.

clue.text: Doubting Thomas Cook's opening putrid stores

indicators.note: to store something is to keep it inside

parts.note: start of SEPTIC
rest of SEPTIC

indicators.note: the opening of a word is where it starts, so its first letter

parts.note: first letter of Cook

explanation.surface: Holidaymakers doubt Thomas Cook after its new branch smells off.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Cook was a British travel agency, but here Doubting Thomas is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A doubting Thomas refuses to believe without proof, like the apostle.

clue.text: Ruddy duck free to shelter under fantail's wings

indicators.note: to shelter under means sitting below, so in this down clue the letters come after the wing letters
wings are the outer edges, so the first and last letters of the bird's name are taken

parts.note: the fantail's wings are those of the word fantail
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, O
to rid is to free

explanation.surface: A duck hides beneath a fantail pigeon's wings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruddy duck' reads as a bird name, but 'Ruddy' is the definition and 'duck' is the cricket zero.
explanation.definitionFit: Florid means having a red or flushed complexion, which is what ruddy describes.

clue.text: God accordingly defends old temple

parts.note: Pan is the Greek god of the wild

indicators.note: defends means guards on both sides, so the word for accordingly surrounds the letter for old

parts.note: then means accordingly, as a result

explanation.surface: A god therefore protects an ancient shrine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'God' looks like the definition, with temple the wordplay; it is the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pantheon is the ancient Roman temple to all the gods, so it is a temple.

clue.text: Big beast in fashion work turned up

parts.note: hip means fashionable, in fashion

indicators.note: turned up means flipped upwards, so in this down clue the word for work is read from the bottom

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A huge animal appears in a fashion show.
explanation.walkthrough: HIP is fashionable; OP (opus, a work) read upwards is PO.
explanation.definitionFit: Hippo is short for hippopotamus, a huge African river animal.

clue.text: Blair, when writing, wore out Liberals

indicators.note: out means wrong or in disarray, so the letters of wore are rearranged

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for Liberal; two Liberals give LL

explanation.surface: Tony Blair wore down the Liberals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blair' suggests Tony Blair; it is Eric Blair, who wrote as George Orwell.
explanation.definitionFit: George Orwell was the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair, author of 1984.

clue.text: The Four Tops in concert are gladly extemporising a set of bars

indicators.note: take the tops, the first letters, of the next four words

parts.note: first letters of Concert Are Gladly Extemporising

explanation.surface: The Motown group the Four Tops happily improvise a few bars on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The Four Tops were an American soul group; here they tell you to take four initial letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A cage is built from a grid of metal bars, so the musical bars of the surface become iron ones.

clue.text: Princess in an opera, not a princess in an operetta

indicators.note: 'not' excludes what follows, so the letter A is removed

parts.note: Aida, Verdi's Ethiopian princess
the letter A, removed

explanation.surface: A trivia line contrasting an opera princess with an operetta one.
explanation.walkthrough: Aida is Verdi's princess; Princess Ida is the Gilbert and Sullivan operetta. The repeated 'princess' is deliberate.
explanation.definitionFit: Ida is the title princess of Gilbert and Sullivan's Princess Ida.

clue.text: Ale bottles on part of sink in standard sizes

indicators.note: bottles means the second ale holds the other pieces inside it

parts.note: start of PORTER, a dark ale
re = on, about
a tap is part of a sink

explanation.surface: Beer bottles standing on the draining board.
explanation.walkthrough: Pret-a-porter is fashion's French term for ready-to-wear clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A fashion-trade term: ready-to-wear clothes are sold off the peg in set sizes rather than made to measure.

clue.text: City with zero money deserted by one banking on thrift

indicators.note: banks line a river on both sides, so the wordplay's letters flank ON

parts.note: EC is the postcode of the City of London
O = zero
MONEY with ONE taken from its middle
ON as printed, banked between EC and O

explanation.surface: A city loses its money when someone who was counting on thrift leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: The ONE removed is literally the letters O, N, E in the middle of M-ONE-Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Economy means thrift, careful spending.

clue.text: Were attractive books bound by European and decorated?

definitions.note: ENTICED is transitive (drew in); 'were attractive' is intransitive, a loose fit

indicators.note: something bound is tied up on both sides

parts.note: E = European
a cake is decorated by icing
NT = New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A question whether European-bound, decorated books looked appealing.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: enticed normally needs an object.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: to entice is to lure, so things that enticed exerted an attraction.
